subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 31-year-old man is rescued after being trapped under a collapsed wall for 6 hours. He has tensely swollen, tender thighs, and his urine is dark brown. Urinalysis is positive for blood but shows no red blood cells on microscopy. Serum creatine kinase is 60,000 U/L, and creatinine is rising despite fluid resuscitation.
question: Which of the following creatine kinase isoenzymes is the predominant form released in this patient?
explanation_correct: Creatine kinase is a dimer of M and B subunits, and CK-MM is the isoenzyme that predominates in skeletal muscle, accounting for most of the CK activity in normal serum. Massive crush injury with rhabdomyolysis releases CK-MM into the circulation, and the resulting myoglobin produces the dipstick-positive, red-cell-free urine that can precipitate acute kidney injury. CK-MB is found mainly in myocardium and CK-BB mainly in brain.

explanation_incorrect.A: CK-MB is predominantly a myocardial isoenzyme; it may rise slightly after severe skeletal muscle injury but is not the predominant form released from damaged muscle.
explanation_incorrect.B: CK-BB is the brain isoenzyme and is not the source of the markedly elevated CK in crush injury.
explanation_incorrect.C: CK-MB2 is a microheterogeneous form of the myocardial isoenzyme used in some assays for early infarction detection, not the main isoenzyme of skeletal muscle.
explanation_incorrect.D: Mitochondrial CK is not the major circulating isoform measured in clinical assays and does not account for the massive CK elevation of rhabdomyolysis.

educationalObjective: CK-MM predominates in skeletal muscle, so rhabdomyolysis from crush injury releases CK-MM along with myoglobin, which can cause acute kidney injury.
